opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so with Canvas, the core question was: when should the model actually open a canvas versus just answering in chat? That sounds simple, but it's really a behavior problem. If the model triggers it too eagerly, it's annoying. You ask a quick question and suddenly there's a whole side panel. If it's too conservative, people never discover the feature. So a lot of the early work was defining what good behavior looks like: writing a long-form document or a substantial piece of code probably warrants a canvas, while a short factual answer doesn't.

From there, we thought about it as a set of core behaviors we wanted the model to learn. One was triggering the canvas at the right moments. Another was editing. When a user asks for a change, does the model rewrite the whole document, or does it make targeted edits to the relevant section? Users usually want the latter, so we had to teach the model when to do a full rewrite and when to do precise, surgical edits. And then commenting: the model gives inline feedback on someone's writing or code the way a thoughtful collaborator would, rather than just taking over.

A big part of how we did it was synthetic data. Instead of relying only on human-collected demonstrations, we used stronger models to generate training data for these specific behaviors, and then built evaluations for each one. We'd measure things like trigger accuracy, edit quality, and comment usefulness, and iterate quickly. That let a pretty small team move fast, because we weren't bottlenecked on collecting huge amounts of human data for every new behavior.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that product and research were very tightly coupled. The model behavior wasn't something we designed in isolation and then handed to the product team. The interface shaped what behaviors mattered, and what the model could do shaped the interface. To me, that's the interesting future of this work: treating model behavior as a product surface you design deliberately, not just a side effect of training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Canvas was interesting because it was really the first time we were trying to teach the model to collaborate on an artifact rather than just answer in a chat stream. And that turned out to be a pretty different behavioral problem than it sounds like.

The way I think about it, there were basically three core behaviors we had to get right. The first was the triggering decision: when should the model open a canvas at all? If someone asks a quick question, you don't want a whole document popping up. But if they say "help me write a blog post" or "let's work on this function," then it should. And that's genuinely a judgment call, because people don't phrase things cleanly. So a lot of the early work was just building really good evaluations around that boundary, with lots of edge cases, and then iterating until the model's intuition matched what users actually expected.

The second behavior was editing. Once you're in a canvas, the default should be targeted edits, not rewriting the whole thing. That sounds obvious, but models at the time had a strong prior toward regenerating everything from scratch, which is really frustrating if you've already spent time on a draft and the model just blows it away. So we had to teach it to be surgical: preserve the user's voice, change only what was asked, and know when a full rewrite is actually warranted versus when it's destructive.

And the third was comments and suggestions, which is more like being a good editor than being a writer. The model has to read something, form opinions about structure or clarity or correctness, and then express those in a way that's actually useful and not just generic feedback like "consider adding more detail."

The thing I'd emphasize is that almost all of this was done with synthetic data generation and distillation from a stronger model. We used o1-preview at the time to generate high-quality demonstrations of these behaviors, and then trained GPT-4o on that. And honestly the hardest part wasn't any one behavior, it was the evals. We built something like a thousand internal evals just for canvas behaviors, because you can't improve what you can't measure, and "the model is a good collaborator" is a very fuzzy target until you decompose it.

The other thing I'd say is that we tried really hard to iterate with real users early. Research intuition only gets you so far, and a lot of what makes something feel good to collaborate with is only visible when actual people are using it in their own workflows.

astra-6.text:
I approached it as a collaboration problem: when should the model make a change, and when should it step back and let the user steer? In a chat interface, you’re usually generating another response. With Canvas, you’re working together on something that already exists, so preserving the user’s intent becomes especially important.

That means thinking about the scope of an edit. If you ask me to improve one paragraph, I shouldn’t rewrite the whole document. And if you’re asking for feedback, a comment might be more useful than immediately changing your work. The behavior I’d want is a collaborator who understands what you’re trying to do, makes the right-sized contribution, and leaves you in control.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: when you’re working on something with a model, what should collaboration feel like? In a chat, the model can just give you another answer. In a canvas, you have an artifact you’re developing together, so it has to be more thoughtful about what to change and what to preserve.

That means thinking about when to make a targeted edit, when a broader rewrite would help, and when to ask you a question. If you highlight one paragraph, that’s a strong signal about where you want attention. The model should respect that scope.

For me, the interesting part is that helpfulness doesn’t always mean doing more. Sometimes it means making a small, precise change and leaving you in control of the rest.
